title: The Colonel in the Garden of Allah
description: The Colonel in the Garden of Allah , 1972 signed, titled and dated 'Joan Brown "The Colonel in the Garden of Allah" July 19, 1972' (on the reverse) enamel on Masonite 90 x 48 1/8 in. 228.6 x 122.2 cm.
provenance: The Colonel | Estate of Joan Brown | Private Collection, New York | | Exhibited | New York, Frumkin/Adams Gallery, Joan Brown: Major Works from the Early 1970s, 13 October-14 November 1992 | West Hartford, Joseloff Gallery, University of Hartford, Joan Brown: Paintings and Drawings from the 1970's, May-June 1993 | New York, George Adams Gallery, Joan Brown: Paintings and Drawings - Three Decades, 1 July-14 August 1998, no. 1 | New York, George Adams Gallery, Joan Brown: Cats and Dogs, 5 April-19 May 2001 | New York, George Adams Gallery, Joan Brown: Friends and Family: Selected Paintings 1970-1973, 4 September-18 October 2009, no. 2 | East Hampton, Eric Firestone Gallery, Go Figure! Curated by Beth Rudin DeWoody, 25 May-22 June 2019 | | Literature | Vivien Raynor, "ART; Back East, a California-Born Master of the Deadpan", The New York Times, 6 June 1993, p. 13 | | Beloved for her vibrant and playful portraits, Joan Brown often explored her personal experiences and the characters in her life through her painting. A quintessential example of Brown's signature style of portraiture, the present lot features her striking ability to infuse her work with personal narrative, spirituality, and art historical significance in a creative alchemy that has led to her being one of the most respected Bay Area artists. | | The subject of the present lot, the Colonel, is shown sitting on the sundeck at San Francisco's historic Dolphin Club, clad in summer attire and leisurely enjoying a glass of red wine. Brown, an avid swimmer, also frequented the Club although it did not officially extend membership to women until 1976 following a lawsuit brought by a collective of six women including Brown herself. Despite this barrier, the Club and the community surrounding it was a sanctuary for Brown, as the title of the work, The Colonel in the Garden of Allah suggests. The reference to the Garden of Allah also speaks to Brown's interest in Arabic cultures and mythology, an interest which would lead her to a deeply impactful visit to Egypt in 1977. | | A 1975 self-portrait, entitled The Night Before the Alcatraz Swim and illustrated on the opposite page also shows Brown seated inside the Dolphin Club on the eve of her first attempt to complete the Alcatraz Swim. While Brown did go on to complete several successful swims from Alcatraz, this first attempt was nearly fatal and left a deep scar on the artist's psyche, leading her to process the trauma in a meditative series of self-portraits. Nevertheless, Brown's love of swimming and the open waters of the San Francisco Bay continued to inspire many of her works including the following lot, Mary Julia #28. | | While Brown had great living mentors, namely Elmer Nelson Bischoff, she was also a devoted student of the Old Masters such as Rembrandt van Rijn, Diego Velázquez, and other giants of the art historical canon including Titian and Ingres. Under this historical lens, the present lot can be viewed as a lighthearted nod to a centuries-old tradition of portraiture in which a nobleman or aristocrat is accompanied by a furry four-legged creature to signal their socioeconomic status or as a symbol of loyalty and devotion. Indeed, dogs and cats feature frequently and prominently throughout Brown's work of the 1970s into the 80s as she began infusing her spirituality into her work, reflecting on fundamental questions about human nature and the dualities that govern it. The bird and cat flanking each of the Colonel's feet like vigilant sentinels have been said to represent the peaceable kingdom, emphasizing the animals' roles as spiritual guardians and stewards of harmony, as well as our duty as humans to peacefully coexist with them. | | The Colonel and the Garden of Allah represents Brown right at home in her element, painting a friend and fellow swimmer in one of her favorite hangouts, surrounded by life in the vibrantly green potted plants and watchful animals. It is a tribute to the community she and the Colonel were proud to be a part of. | | Joan Brown's work is represented in the collections of notable institutions including the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; the Berkeley Art Museum; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; and the Los Angeles County Museum among others. Brown was the subject of a major retrospective exhibition at SFMOMA in 2022.
